Posted June 19, 2005
Analysis by Richard Cowan

I like George Will. I dont always agree with him, as we shall see, but he is literate, civil and has a sense of history. All of these qualities are sorely lacking in the Howler Monkey generation of political commentary: whoever gets the furthest out on a limb and makes the most noise is an "opinion leader."

In 1972, I first began to urge American conservatives, specifically those associated with National Review magazine for which Will wrote at the time, to apply the same political and intellectual standards to the marijuana question that they applied to every other issue.
See
The Police Fraud. Someone Is Lying. Marking The 30th Anniversary Of An Article in National Review. What if Don Quixote Was Right? Analysis by Richard Cowan
and
Exclusive To MarijuanaNews: Interview With William F. Buckley, Jr. By Noah Pollak and Dan Mindus

I would like to take credit for what ensued, but the fact is that I was generally heard only by those whose libertarian inclinations overcame their cultural distaste for the cultural baggage which they (wrongly, I think) attributed to cannabis. I was merely a catalyst. Alas, Will did not turn out to be among that number that followed suit..

Now, half a lifetime later, Wills persistent prohibitionism has manifested itself in that ultimate act of intellectual self-degradation, quoting John Walters without checking the facts. He simply cannot follow history, his own principles, and the realities at hand.

First, it should be noted that it is a very odd newspaper practice for each editorial page to make up its own headline or title for syndicated columns. Thus, Wills mid-June prohibitionist relapse ran under titles that reflect the editors rather than the authors choice. In the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, it was Marijuana's Reputation Too Benign. However, in Wills hometown paper, The Washington Post, it was This War Is Worth Fighting.

From the Washington Post
June 16, 2005; A29
This War Is Worth Fighting.
By George F. Will
georgewill@washpost.com

Exasperated by pessimism about the "war on drugs," John Walters, director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy, says: Washington is awash with lobbyists hired by businesses worried that government may, intentionally or inadvertently, make them unprofitable. So why assume that trade in illicit drugs is the one business that government, try as it might, cannot seriously injure?
(MarijuanaNews note: Because the drugwar is counterproductive.)
See
Program Notes for the MarijuanaNews World Report for May 26, 2005 Drugwar Makes Things Worse. CIA Drug Watchlist; Meth, Violence in Mexico; Drugs From Quebec? Narks and Smuggling; China Needs Help?
and
Giulianis Police State  Like the Marijuana Prohibition That He Loves  Is A Counterproductive Fraud. 3 Articles.

Here is why: When Pat Moynihan was an adviser to President Richard Nixon, he persuaded the French government to break the "French connection" by which heroin came to America. Moynihan explained his achievement to Labor Secretary George Shultz, who said laconically: "Good."

Moynihan: "No, really, this is a big event."

Shultz, unfazed: "Good."

Moynihan: "I suppose that you think that so long as there is a demand for drugs, there will continue to be a supply."

Shultz: "You know, there's hope for you yet."
(MarijuanaNews note: Two points here.

First, Will clearly understands Shultzs argument. George Shultz, former Secretary of Labor and of State and other offices and very much a part of the Republican establishment, is an anti-prohibitionist.

The late Pat Moynihan was a very decent and intelligent moderate Democrat, but he could never make that leap. Agreeing with Moynihan is one thing, but for Will to agree with Donna Shalala, Clintons appalling and very liberal Secretary of HHS, is something else.
See
"New War On Drugs Has Familiar Ring," Says Ottawa Citizen; "There is no such thing as a soft drug," Says Shalala

Second, having granted Shultzs premise that supply will answer demand, Will must either oppose the drugwar, or support demand reduction  arresting millions of Americans. So, he explains Walters thinking.)

Walters understands that when there is a $65 billion annual American demand for an easily smuggled commodity produced in poor countries, and when the price of cocaine and heroin on U.S. streets is 100 times the production costs, much will evade even sophisticated interdiction methods. And, Walters says, huge quantities of marijuana are grown domestically, for example, in California, Kentucky and West Virginia -- often on public lands because the government can seize private land used for marijuana cultivation. And particularly potent strains of the drug are grown indoors. Marijuana possession, not trafficking, accounts for most of the surge in drug arrests since 1990. Critics suggest an armistice on this front in the $35 billion-a-year drug war.
(MarijuanaNews note: To his credit, Will acknowledges this fact, but omits the crucial numbers. Marijuana possession arrests are around 700,000 per year, almost half of all drug arrests.)
See
Program Notes for the MarijuanaNews World Report, May 5, 2005. Montel Williams Appeals to Congress, Blairs Reefer Madness, Washington Post Puts Arrest Data on Front Page! NORMLs Allen St. Pierre.
and
NORMLs arrest report

Marijuana's price has fallen and its potency has doubled in the past eight years. So say David Boyum and Peter Reuter in their new book, "An Analytic Assessment of U.S. Drug Policy," from the American Enterprise Institute. They say that although the number of people incarcerated for drug offenses on any given day has increased from 50,000 in 1980 to 450,000 in 2003, the inflation-adjusted prices for cocaine and heroin are half of what they were 25 years ago.
(MarijuanaNews note:Will does not address the critics who suggest an armistice in a war that takes 700,000 prisoners a year, instead he lets the Czar change the subject.)

So, should there be an armistice on this front, too? Walters responds that the bulk of the demand for illegal drugs is from addictive users. Of the 19 million users, 7 million are drug-dependent.
(MarijuanaNews note: Oh really?

First, it is not clear that Walters response is relevant to the answer. If the bulk of the demand for illegal drugs is from addictive users, does that mean necessarily mean that we have to keep arresting them? It does not seem to be solving the problem.

For one thing, this says nothing about the illegal use of prescription drugs. Between 1995 and 2002, there was a 163 percent increase in the number of emergency-room visits tied to the abuse of prescription drugs. Prescription drugs are now a factor in a quarter of all overdose deaths reported in the United States.
See
 John Walters Says, Prescription Drug Abuse Is The Second Largest Illicit Drug Problem  After Cannabis, Of Course! Different Measures for Success and Failure. Seeking New Victims.

Second, is it true that the bulk of the demand for illegal drugs is from addictive users. And Of the 19 million users, 7 million are drug-dependent.?

According to a 2000 Drug Czars office report: Excluding persons in custody, between 1988 and 1998, about 3.2 million to 3.9 million Americans were hardcore users of cocaine and  630,000 to 980,000 Americans were hardcore users of heroin Considering the overlap between hardcore cocaine users and hardcore heroin users, the estimates suggest that there were about 3.3 million hardcore users of heroin or cocaine in 1998.

Of course, Walters says millions of casual marijuana users are dependent.)
See
 Walters Tells a New Lie. Oh Happy Day! People Need Treatment If They Are Sent to Treatment, By Definition. And How Do They Treat Marijuana Addicts? We Couldnt Make This Up, But They Did.

Marijuana use is a "pediatric onset" problem: If people get past their teens without starting, Walters says, the probability of use is "very small" and the likelihood of dependence "much less."
(MarijuanaNews note: First, if that is true, why are we arresting adults to prevent teens from using marijuana? 

Second, the term Walters used was actually pediatric onsetdisease. It is ironic that that Will wouldnt choke on such psychobabble. In December of 1999, Will wrote an excellent column deploring the over-prescribing of Ritalin to boys.

In it, he cites Paul R.  McHugh, professor of psychiatry at Johns Hopkins University:
"Psychiatric conditions are routinely differentiated by appearances alone," even when it is "difficult to distinguish symptoms of illness from normal variations in human life," or from the normal responses of sensitive people to life's challenges.  But if a condition can be described, it can be named; once named, a distinct disorder can be linked to a particular treatment.

(Like arresting people???)

The idea that most individuals deficient in attentiveness or confidence are sick encourages what McHugh calls pharmacological "mental cosmetics." This "should be offensive to anyone who values the richness of human psychological diversity.  Both medically and morally, encumbering this naturally occurring diversity with the terminology of disease is a first step toward efforts, however camouflaged, to control it."

So, by calling cannabis use a pediatric onset disease the Czar would treat it by arresting not only minors, but also adults. At least the makers of Ritalin do not have the power to arrest and thereby coerce potential customers yet.)
See
DEAland Children Consume 90% of the Worlds Ritalin. "This year six million children across the USA -- over one tenth of the schoolage population -- will be prescribed anti-depressants and stimulants." Context for The Medical Marijuana Debate and "Drug Education"

Use of marijuana by youths peaked in 1979, hit a low in 1992 and then doubled by the mid-'90s. The age of first use of marijuana has been declining to the early teens and lower. Often, Walters says, the "triggers" for use are "cultural messages" -- today, for example, from rap music.
(MarijuanaNews note: Before that it was rock music; and before that it was jazz and swing: "There are 100,000 total marijuana smokers in the US, and most are Negroes, Hispanics, Filipinos and entertainers. Their Satanic music, jazz and swing, result from marijuana usage. This marijuana causes white women to seek sexual relations with Negroes, entertainers and any others."   Harry Anslinger, U.S. Commissioner of Narcotics, testifying to Congress on why marijuana should be made illegal, 1937.)

Nevertheless, teen marijuana use has declined 18 percent in the past three years.
(MarijuanaNews note: Why? Did someone turn down the Satanic music? Or was this just a statistical artifact? What is the margin of error? And what does this really tell us about the success of the drugwar as a whole?
See
Again the Media Parrots the Partnerships Prohibitionist Propaganda Even Though Reported "Changes" Are Within the Margin of Error. Emphasis in Propaganda as in Seizures Shows Drug War Really About Mar

First, the rate of teen marijuana is much lower in The Netherlands than it is in DEAland.
See
Dutch Lessons: Tolerance Works. Prohibition Is Counterproductive. Who Is The Real Threat To Our Freedom and Security?

Second, is this really the measure of success?

The Washington Post reported on December 22nd of last year, For the third straight year, illegal drug use by teenagers declined slightly in 2004 -- with the notable exceptions of inhalants, alcohol and the painkiller OxyContin, government investigators said yesterday.

Since 2001, the number of high school students who reported using an illicit drug in the past month fell 17 percent to 16.1 percent this year. Teenagers saying they had used alcohol within the past 30 days declined 7.7 percent to 33 percent.

Overall, high school seniors reported using a broader array of illegal substances with more frequency. Fully 70 percent of 12th-graders said they have consumed alcoholic beverages during the past year, and 52 percent reported having been drunk at least once in 2004.

Since the 2000 election cycle, the beer, wine and liquor industries have contributed more than $35 million to federal candidates, about 60 percent of it to Republicans, according to analysis by the nonpartisan Center for Responsive Politics.

But there was a noticeable increase in inhalant use by younger teenagers These include glues, paint thinner, nail polish remover, gasoline and shoe polish

Last year, John Walters crowed that teen marijuana use was declining, and this proved that the Drug War is enjoying yet one more great victory. The occasion was the latest survey (PATS Study 2003  Teens) by The Partnership For A Drug-Free America, which claimed that over the past five years, there had been a seven percent decline (from 42 to 39 percent in one-time teen marijuana use.)

Then we are told, If the decline had not occurred, 760,000 more teens would have tried marijuana than is currently the case." 

Thus, the "seven percent decline (from 42 to 39 percent)" claimed for marijuana is actually just three percentage points, which is within the plus or minus 1.5% margin of error. So there may not have been any change at all.

For example, a drop from 10% to 8% is two percentage points, but a 20% change. If the margin of error is greater than difference then the numbers may not mean anything at all. Watch for the margin of errors in the Presidential polls.

Thus, over a five-year period, more than 3 million Americans of all ages were arrested on marijuana charges to prevent a possible 760,000 teens from trying marijuana once. The 3 million are real. The 760,000 are speculative.)

Because marijuana is, unlike heroin and cocaine, not toxic -- because marijuana users do not die from overdoses -- its reputation is too benign. The 5 million users in the 12-to-17 age cohort are, Walters believes, storing up future family, school and work problems and putting their brain functions at risk with increasingly potent strains of marijuana.
(MarijuanaNews note: First, where are the "victims" of the last four decades of marijuana use? In the White House, the Senate, the Supreme Court?

Second, notice the continued success of the new potent pot line.)
See
 Dan Forbes Documents Walters Lies About Potency. Understanding That The War On Cannabis Is Built On Lies Is Key to Understanding More Than Just Drug War.

Many of these strains -- and perhaps one-third of the total U.S. marijuana supply -- come from Canada. A few years ago police estimated that there were 10,000 growers in the Toronto metropolitan area.

(MarijuanaNews note: No, that was this year. In February of 2005, the National Post reported that Ontario Safety Minister Monte Kwinter claimed, "We have as many grow-ops in metro Toronto as the United States". But Mr.  Kwinter provided any statistics to back up their claims regarding Toronto grow-ops.

And as for Walters claim that perhaps one-third of the total U.S. marijuana supply -- come from Canada Well, as Ronald Reagan would say, there he goes again. Seizures at the Canadian border  the only hard data  are less than 2% of seizures at the Mexican border.)
See
As Canada Moves Toward Some Form Of Decriminalization, Canadian Narks and Walters Escalate Lying. The New Math. Canada Replaces Mexico As Leading Supplier of Cannabis. And If You Believe That
and
Time Magazine Reports BC Bud 20% Less Potent Than Four Years Ago??  Incompetent Prohibitionist Propaganda and Even Worse Journalism. As Some Reporters Die to Find the Truth Others Live to Lie.

Last year 400 metric tons of cocaine were seized worldwide, but at least 200 entered the United States. However, some seizures, by causing abrupt shortages in some metropolitan areas, cause addicts to seek detoxification. Walters says that breaking the French connection did that in New York in 1972. Even Prohibition, he says, for all its bad effects, changed behavior: After repeal, per capita alcohol use did not return to pre-Prohibition levels until the 1960s.
(MarijuanaNews note: I said that I liked Wills sense of history, but references that are a bit more contemporary would be good.)

Walters says the data do not support the theory that society has a "latent level of substance abuse" -- that if one problem declines, another rises commensurately. And he thinks indifference to drug abuse, which debilitates the individual's capacity to flourish in freedom, mocks the nation's premises.
(MarijuanaNews note: Whereas arresting millions of peaceful cannabis users upholds the nations premises?

Having studied political philosophy at the University of Toronto with the late Allan Bloom, Walters describes the drug war in Lincolnian language: "There are certain requirements of civilization -- to keep the better angels of our nature in preponderance over the lesser angels."
(MarijuanaNews note: Do our better angels lie at every turn to justify arresting people?
See
Walters Puts The Media to the Test By Taking Hyper-Lying to A New Level. Blood Libels To Justify Police State. San Diego Medical Activist Faces Federal Charges for 20 Plants.

Do our better angels lie to justify arresting sick and dying people?)
See
 Reading Between The Lies. New Version of An Old Lie About My Saying Medical Cannabis Is A Scam May Be Clue to New Prohibitionist Party Line. Only A Few Hundred Patients?

Fighting terrorists, he says, is necessary even though it is like seeking a needle in a haystack. Illicit drugs -- millions of pounds marketed to millions of Americans -- are at least not a needle-in-a-haystack problem.
See
Mexico, the Drugwar and the US National Interest: Never Mind Iraq; We Need To Pay Attention to What We Are Doing to Our Southern Neighbor.

(MarijuanaNews note: In the 17 September 17th, 2001 issue of  Newsweek, Will wrote, We Need More Sensible Standards For Deciding If Drug Policies Are, Or Are Not, 'Working'

We do need some new policies--but we also need a more sensible notion of what constitutes "working." Here success comes only in shades of gray, but is not for that reason derisory.

Wills did not elicit from Walters any definition of success. In stead, he simply took his lies at face value. As Sir Francis Bacon said, We prefer to believe what we prefer to be true.

Clearly, Wills wants to believe in prohibition, and that marijuanas reputation is too benign. But it is time for Will to practice what he so eloquently preached in his May 5, 2004 column: "Time for Bush to see the realities of Iraq:

This administration cannot be trusted to govern if it cannot be counted on to think and, having thought, to have second thoughts...

Being steadfast in defense of carefully considered convictions is a virtue. Being blankly incapable of distinguishing cherished hopes from disappointing facts, or of reassessing comforting doctrines in face of contrary evidence, is a crippling political vice...

Ron Chernow's magnificent new biography of Alexander Hamilton begins with these of his subject's words: I have thought it my duty to exhibit things as they are, not as they ought to be. That is the core of conservatism.

The most disturbing part of Wills acceptance of the Czars line came when he told us that Walters thinks indifference to drug abuse, which debilitates the individual's capacity to flourish in freedom, mocks the nation's premises.

In 2003, Will observed, (T)he Cold War may come to be remembered as a parenthesis in a much longer war against the remarkable resilience and insufficiently understood variousness of fascism.
See
The Prohibitionist Counterattack in Canada Escalates. Blatant Drive to Create DEAland Style Police State. Phony Decrim Bill Gets Even Worse.

The drugwar is one of those insufficiently understood variousness of fascism. It is an ideology aimed at increasing the power of the state at the expense of the individual.
See
 Calling All Quacks: The Therapeutic Police State and the Politicization of Medicine. Doctors Cannot Study The Violence of Cannabis Prohibition. Because They Are The Disease, Not The Cure.
and
 The Prohibitionist Police State Versus The People. Analysis By Richard Cowan
New Dutch Study on "Licit and illicit drug use in the Netherlands" Shows Why International Anti-Dutch Prohibitionist Propaganda Campaign Is Vital to Drug Warriors. How Ideology Works.

Consider this quote from one who should know:
...The Fascist State organizes the nation, but leaves a sufficient margin of liberty to the individual; the latter is deprived of all useless and possibly harmful freedom, but retains what is essential; the deciding power in this question cannot be the individual, but the State alone....   Benito Mussolini, 1932.)
